entry.content:
Hello and welcome to our website!

Today, we are going to introduce you to the IELTS Reading section. We will show you what the test looks like, explain how you can prepare for it, and introduce you to the different types of questions.

At the end of this article, you will have the opportunity to answer some practice questions and compare your answers with the correct ones.

The life and work of Marie Curie

Marie Curie is probably the most famous woman scientist who has ever lived. Born Maria Sklodowska in Poland in 1867, she is famous for her work on radioactivity, and was twice a winner of the Nobel Prize. With her husband, Pierre Curie, and Henri Becquerel, she was awarded the 1903 Nobel Prize for Physics, and was then sole winner of the 1911 Nobel Prize for Chemistry. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

From childhood, Marie was remarkable for her prodigiousVery large, impressive, or extraordinary in amount or ability. memory, and at the age of 16 won a gold medal on completion of her secondary education. Because her father lost his savings through bad investment, she then had to take work as a teacher. From her earnings she was able to finance her sister Bronia’s medical studies in Paris, on the understanding that Bronia would, in turn, later help her to get an education.

In 1891 this promise was fulfilledCompleted or achieved as promised or expected. and Marie went to Paris and began to study at the Sorbonne (the University of Paris). She often worked far into the night and lived on little more than bread and butter and tea. She came first in the examinationA formal test to measure someone's knowledge or ability. in the physical sciences in 1893, and in 1894ّؤ was placed second in the examination in mathematical sciences. It was not until the spring of that year that she was introduced to Pierّre Curie.

Their marriage in 1895 marked the start of a partnership that was soon to achieve results of world significanceThe importance or meaning of something.. Following Henri Becquerel’s discovery in 1896 of a new phenomenon, which Marie later called ‘radioactivity’, Marie Curie decided to find out if the radioactivity discovered in uranium was to be found in other elements. She discovered that this was true for thorium.

Turning her attention to mineralsNatural substances found in rocks and in the ground., she found her interest drawn to pitchblende, a mineral whose radioactivity, superior to that of pure uranium, could be explained only by the presence in the ore of small quantities of an unknown substance of very high activity. Pierre Curie joined her in the work that she had undertaken to resolve this problem, and that led to the discovery of the new elements, polonium and radium. While Pierre Curie devoted himself chieflyMainly or mostly. to the physical study of the new radiations, Marie Curie struggled to obtainTo get or acquire something. pure radium in the metallic state. This was achieved with the help of the chemist André-Louis Debierne, one of Pierre Curie’s pupils. Based on the results of this research, Marie Curie received her Doctorate of Science, and in 1903 Marie and Pierre shared with Becquerel the Nobel Prize for Physics for the discovery of radioactivity.

The births of Marie’s two daughters, Irène and Eve, in 1897 and 1904 failed to interrupt her scientific work. She was appointed lecturer in physics at the École Normale Supérieure for girls in Sèvres, France (1900), and introduced a method of teaching based on experimental demonstrationsPractical examples or explanations showing how something works.. In December 1904 she was appointed chief assistant in the laboratory directed by Pierre Curie.

The sudden death of her husband in 1906 was a bitter blowA very upsetting or disappointing event. to Marie Curie, but was also a turning point in her career: henceforthFrom this time forward; from now on. she was to devote all her energy to completing alone the scientific work that they had undertaken. On May 13, 1906, she was appointedOfficially chosen for a particular job or position. to the professorshipThe position or job of a professor at a university. that had been left vacant on her husband’s death, becoming the first woman to teach at the Sorbonne. In 1911 she was awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for the isolationThe process of separating something from other substances. of a pure form of radium.

During World War I, Marie Curie, with the help of her daughter Irène, devoted herself to the development of the use of X-radiography, including the mobile units which came to be known as ‘Little Curies’, used for the treatment of wounded soldiers. In 1918 the Radium Institute, whose staff Irène had joined, began to operate in earnest, and became a centre for nuclear physics and chemistry. Marie Curie, now at the highest point of her fame and, from 1922, a member of the Academy of Medicine, researched the chemistry of radioactive substancesParticular types of materials or matter. and their medical applications.

In 1921, accompaniedWent somewhere together with someone. by her two daughters, Marie Curie made a triumphantShowing great success or victory. journey to the United States to raise funds for research on radium. Women there presented her with a gram of radium for her campaignAn organized effort to achieve a particular goal.. Marie also gave lectures in Belgium, Brazil, Spain and Czechoslovakia and, in addition, had the satisfactionA feeling of happiness or pleasure because something has been achieved. of seeing the development of the Curie Foundation in Paris, and the inaugurationThe official opening or beginning of something. in 1932 in Warsaw of the Radium Institute, where her sister Bronia became director.

One of Marie Curie’s outstanding achievements was to have understood the need to accumulateTo collect or gather things over time. intense radioactive sources, not only to treat illness but also to maintainTo keep something in good condition or continue to have it. an abundantExisting in large quantities; more than enough. supply for research. The existence in Paris at the Radium InstituteAn organization created for education, research, or a particular purpose. of a stock of 1.5 grams of radium made a decisiveHaving a major influence on the final result. contributionSomething that a person does or gives to help achieve a result. to the success of the experiments undertaken in the years around 1930. This work prepared the way for the discovery of the neutron by Sir James Chadwick and, above all, for the discovery in 1934 by Irène and Frédéric Joliot-Curie of artificial radioactivity. A few months after this discovery, Marie Curie died as a result of leukaemia caused by exposureThe state of being subjected to something, such as radiation or sunlight. to radiation. She had often carried test tubes containing radioactive isotopes in her pocket, remarking on the pretty blue-green light they gave off.

Her contributionSomething that a person does or gives to help achieve a result. to physics had been immenseExtremely large or great in size, amount, or degree., not only in her own work, the importance of which had been demonstrated by her two Nobel Prizes, but because of her influence on subsequentHappening or coming after something else. generations of nuclear physicists and chemists.

 

Alright! Now, answer the questions that follow.

Before you start, don't worry if you come across unfamiliar words. Try to figure out their meanings from the context, or simply ignore them when they are not important for understanding the passage.

We've highlighted some challenging words in the article, and we'll help you learn their meanings at the end.

IELTS Academic Reading – Practice Questions

Questions 1–6: True, False or Not Given

Choose TRUE if the statement agrees with the information in the passage.

Choose FALSE if the statement contradicts the information.

Choose NOT GIVEN if there is no information about the statement in the passage.

1. Marie Curie’s husband was a joint winner of both Marie’s Nobel Prizes.

  • TRUE

  • FALSE

  • NOT GIVEN

2. Marie became interested in science when she was a child.

  • TRUE

  • FALSE

  • NOT GIVEN

3. Marie was able to attend the Sorbonne because of her sister’s financial contribution.

  • TRUE

  • FALSE

  • NOT GIVEN

4. Marie stopped doing research for several years when her children were born.

  • TRUE

  • FALSE

  • NOT GIVEN

5. Marie took over the teaching position her husband had held.

  • TRUE

  • FALSE

  • NOT GIVEN

6. Marie’s sister Bronia studied the medical uses of radioactivity.

  • TRUE

  • FALSE

  • NOT GIVEN

Questions 7–13: Note Completion

Complete the notes below.

Write ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

Marie Curie's Research on Radioactivity

7. When uranium was discovered to be radioactive, Marie Curie found that the element __________ had the same property.

8. Marie and Pierre Curie’s research into the radioactivity of the mineral known as __________ led to the discovery of two new elements.

9. In 1911, Marie Curie received recognition for her work on the element __________.

10. Marie and Irène Curie developed X-radiography, which was used as a medical technique for __________.

11. Marie Curie saw the importance of collecting radioactive material both for research and for cases of __________.

12. The radioactive material stocked in Paris contributed to the discoveries in the 1930s of the __________ and of what was known as artificial radioactivity.

13. During her research, Marie Curie was exposed to radiation and, as a result, she suffered from __________.

 

Now it's time to compare your answers with the correct ones!

Vocabulary – Learn New Words

Word / Phrase English Definition
Prodigious Very large, impressive, or extraordinary in amount or ability.
Fulfilled Completed or achieved as promised or expected.
Examination A formal test to measure someone's knowledge or ability.
Significance The importance or meaning of something.
Minerals Natural substances found in rocks and in the ground.
Chiefly Mainly or mostly.
Obtain To get or acquire something.
Demonstrations Practical examples or explanations showing how something works.
Bitter blow A very upsetting or disappointing event.
Henceforth From this time forward; from now on.
Appointed Officially chosen for a particular job or position.
Professorship The position or job of a professor at a university.
Isolation The process of separating something from other substances.
Substances Particular types of materials or matter.
Accompanied Went somewhere together with someone.
Triumphant Showing great success or victory.
Campaign An organized effort to achieve a particular goal.
Satisfaction A feeling of happiness or pleasure because something has been achieved.
Inauguration The official opening or beginning of something.
Accumulate To collect or gather things over time.
Maintain To keep something in good condition or continue to have it.
Abundant Existing in large quantities; more than enough.
Institute An organization created for education, research, or a particular purpose.
Decisive Having a major influence on the final result.
Contribution Something that a person does or gives to help achieve a result.
Exposure The state of being subjected to something, such as radiation or sunlight.
Immense Extremely large or great in size, amount, or degree.
Subsequent Happening or coming after something else.
